text: Formulas, sterile equipment, and sampling procedures have been compiled. Production requires basic chemicals, food, and a steady power supply.

Plans for pumps, water networks, and the structural supports of multi-story housing are finalized. Building materials still need to be delivered to the site, where local workers will build it section by section.

Prototype plans for blades, gearboxes, and grid connections are ready. Wind turbines can be built under the “Energy” category in a district or location. They need operators and parts for maintenance, and backup power is still required when the wind is weak.

Plans for boilers, circulation pumps, and insulated piping are ready. Once the heating plant is complete, it still needs operators and a sufficient coal supply. The plant can take over citywide heating once its trial run is stable.

Adds 160 beds when complete; requires existing public healthcare and classroom coverage, and enough water capacity for current residents plus 160 more.
Only upgrades irrigated plots; next round, with enough water, each new farmer produces 2 food. With insufficient water, production falls back to 1.4 food.
Houses up to 12 teachers when complete. Each teacher looks after 20 children, and daily lessons still consume wood.
Adds 2 transport worker positions when complete; dispatching a migration convoy requires 4 transport workers. Residents must have a continuous food supply during construction.

Each set requires 2 wind turbine operators and generates 12 power at rated output. Each operator consumes 0.04 parts every 10 seconds for maintenance. Actual output varies with local wind; turbines stop in still air. A backup power source is required.

Each Heating Station: the electric shift requires 2 heating workers and consumes 1 electricity, 0.8 coal, and 0.02 parts every 10 seconds, heating 600 people; the manual shift requires 4 workers and consumes 1.2 coal and 0.02 parts, heating 300 people. Day-to-day heating can be formally handed over only after the trial run covers everyone.

Each Waterworks Station: the electric shift requires 4 waterworks workers and consumes 4 electricity, supplying water for 600 people; the manual shift requires 8 waterworks workers and supplies water for 300 people. Both methods consume 0.2 chemicals and 0.02 parts each round.
Craftspeople marked deposits of quartz sand, clay, and salts along the edge of an old mine map. We can build an extraction site there.
Collectors brought back sorted mineral feedstock, giving chemical production and glassmaking the materials they need.
The mineral feedstock has been sorted. With old iron cans and firebrick, we can put together a crude chemical reactor.
The chemical workshop has fired up. Production is faster when powered; if the power goes out, coal can keep it simmering.
The ratios of pig iron, furnace charge, and deoxidizer have been recorded in a new process sheet. Wrought iron and old parts are enough to put up a steel furnace frame for now.
Molten steel slowly sets in the mold, glowing dark red. Steelworkers still need a steady supply of iron ingots, coal, chemicals, and maintenance tools.
Quartz and soda ash purified in the chemical workshop have been delivered to the glassmakers. They now have a workable process for making clear vessels and window glass.
